name: Thai Sign Language
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Thai Sign Language (thai1240) is not in the catalog, and both works with stress in the title are Glottolog misattributions: Glottolog 5.1 hangs Tumtavitikul 1998 (SEALS IV, listed as 'Warotamasikkhadit and Panakul 1997', ref 684097) and Potisuk, Gandour & Harper 1994 (LTBA 17.2, ref 177821) on thai1240 because their titles say 'Thai', but both are about spoken Standard/Bangkok Thai (thai1261), where Glottolog also lists the same works (8693, 8686, 675826) and our already holds Potisuk 1994. I downloaded the full SEALang SALA scan of Tumtavitikul 1998 (20 pp, scanned at 300 dpi; and read its stress section: for spoken Thai, primary stress is always word-final, non-final syllables are stressed by weight, derived by right-headed leftward unbounded feet (pp. 63-65). Potisuk 1994 (same file already held by the project under thai1261, byte-identical) is an acoustic study of Bangkok Thai compound stress. Neither says anything about a sign language, so no first-hand stress statement for Thai Sign Language was found (no new stress statement was found). Crossref title searches for 'Thai Sign Language' (40 rows) and 'Thai Sign Language prosody/stress' (14 rows) returned nothing on prosody or stress in TSL; the Glottolog thai1240 page cites no phonology work. Recommended action: re-point Glottolog 684097 and 177821 to thai1261 in our per-language bibliography; the scanned Tumtavitikul 1998 text is now available for the spoken-Thai search. written in the thai1240 folder.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Only one work is listed for this item and it was opened; no listed work was marked not-opened. As the required spot-check of silent material I re-a full-text search for stress/accent the four earlier-pass files in the same folder for stress/accent/prominence/prosody/intonation/rhythm terms (English and Thai): Tumtavitikul & Niwatapant 2008 (rsj4-1..) only compares facial expression to 'prosody or suprasegment' in spoken-language phonetics (line 79, journal p. 97) and uses จังหวะ for the two-beat approaching-movement/hold sequence of a sign syllable, no stress statement; Tumtavitikul, Niwatapant & Dill 2009 (skase.. line 635) mentions 'stress, tone, intonation, duration' only as examples of…

sources.citation: Suwanarat, Manfa & Charles Reilly (comps.), with A. Ratanasint, L. Anderson & O. Wrigley. 1986. The Thai Sign Language Dictionary, Book One. Bangkok: National Association of the Deaf in Thailand. (ERIC ED275204)
sources.note: scanned of the archive.org ERIC microfiche, a full-text search for stress/accent and the movement/verb-grammar notes read: only 'rhythms of basic movements' symbols and a note (p. 145) that repetition and 'changes in rhythm of motion' change lexical meaning. No notion of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Suppasin, Nattawit, Kunlaya Sai-Ngam & Paruhut Premsamit. 2026. The Grammatical Structure of Thai Sign Language: An Analysis at the Phrase, Sentence, and Discourse Levels. Journal of Ratchasuda Institute for Research and Development of Persons with Disabilities 22(1): 122-137.
sources.note: Phrase/sentence/discourse syntax synthesis (Thai). Nothing on phonology or stress; useful for its reference list, which supplied the open URL of Tumtavitikul & Niwatapant 2008 and the repository handles of Danthanavanich 2008 and Niwatapant 2006.

sources.citation: Tumtavitikul, Apiluck, Chirapa Niwatapant & Philipp Dill. 2009. Classifiers in Thai Sign Language. SKASE Journal of Theoretical Linguistics 6(1): 27-44. [Glottolog 35076]
sources.note: Classifier morphology only; a brief sec. 2 recap that TSL syllables have nucleus + peripheral units 'comparable to vowels and consonants'. The only mention of stress (p. 38) is generic: spoken languages layer 'stress, tone, intonation, duration' onto segments, contrasted with simultaneity in sign. No TSL stress statement.

sources.citation: Danthanavanich, Suksiri. 2008. A grammar of Thai Sign Language. PhD thesis, Mahidol University (Ratchasuda College), xix+225 pp.
sources.note: The only full grammar of TSL; a phonology chapter (if any) is the likeliest place for any remark on prominence/stress or its absence.

sources.citation: Tumtavitikul, Apiluck & Jirapa Niwatapant. 2008. พยางค์และคำในภาษามือไทย / Syllables and Words in Thai Sign Language. Journal of Ratchasuda College for Research and Development of Persons with Disabilities 4(1): 95-113.
sources.note: Read in full (16 pp, Thai). The primary phonological description of TSL: hand-units (handshape, orientation, location, movement, non-manuals) with minimal pairs; syllable = movement as nucleus by 'visual sonority' (after Brentari/Wilbur/Perlmutter); syllable reduction/deletion, assimilation, non-dominant-hand deletion; word types. Nothing on stress or accent. The only prosodic remark (sec. 1.1.1, p. 3 = journal p. 97) is a general sign-language model statement that facial expression 'can be compared to prosody or suprasegmentals (สัทสัมพันธ์) in spoken-language phonetics'; 'strong/weak hand'…

sources.citation: Tumtavitikul, Apiluck. 1998 [1997]. The metrical structure of Thai in a non-linear perspective. SEALS IV (1994), 53-72 [and Abramson (ed.) 1997, 309-324]. [Glottolog 684097, attached to thai1240]
sources.note: Held from the crashed verification (downloaded from SEALang SALA and scanned). Concerns SPOKEN Standard Thai (thai1261): weight-sensitive metrical structure, heavy syllables attract stress. Glottolog misattributes it to Thai Sign Language; it says nothing about any sign language and must not be used for thai1240.
